claim: Rapid morphological evolution (tempo) is associated with mechanical sensitivity (strong correlation between a mechanical system's output and one or more of its components) across multiple four-bar linkage systems in animals.
source: Across multiple four-bar linkage systems in animals, we discovered that rapid morphological evolution (tempo) is associated with mechanical sensitivity (strong correlation between a mechanical system's output and one or more of its components).
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study, and it is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and Table 1 showing evolutionary rates and mechanical sensitivity correlations across four different four-bar linkage systems.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity is explained by size: the smallest link(s) are disproportionately affected by length changes and most strongly influence mechanical output.
source: Mechanical sensitivity is explained by size: the smallest link(s) are disproportionately affected by length changes and most strongly influence mechanical output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the Discussion section with biomechanical explanations about how length changes in small links have proportionally larger effects.

claim: Rate of evolutionary change (tempo) is greatest in the smallest links.
source: Rate of evolutionary change (tempo) is greatest in the smallest links and trait shifts across phylogeny (mode) occur exclusively via the influential, small links.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by evolutionary rate data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Trait shifts across phylogeny (mode) occur exclusively via the influential, small links.
source: Rate of evolutionary change (tempo) is greatest in the smallest links and trait shifts across phylogeny (mode) occur exclusively via the influential, small links.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the Bayesian analysis of trait shifts in wrasses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tempo and mode are dominated by strong correlations that exemplify mechanical sensitivity, even in linkage systems known for exhibiting many-to-one mapping.
source: Our findings illuminate the paradigms of many-to-one mapping, mechanical sensitivity, and constraints: tempo and mode are dominated by strong correlations that exemplify mechanical sensitivity, even in linkage systems known for exhibiting many-to-one mapping.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a synthesis of the findings, supported by data showing both many-to-one mapping and mechanical sensitivity patterns.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity imparts distinct, predictable footprints on morphological diversity.
source: Amidst myriad influences, mechanical sensitivity imparts distinct, predictable footprints on morphological diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the consistent patterns observed across multiple independent four-bar linkage systems.

claim: The uneven tempo of phenotypic evolution is a universal feature of biological systems, from proteins to whole-organism traits.
source: The uneven tempo of phenotypic evolution is a universal feature of biological systems, from proteins to whole-organism traits (Simpson, 1944; Gingerich, 2009; Zhang and Yang, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on evolutionary tempo.

claim: Rates of morphological divergence and speciation are often coupled.
source: Because rates of morphological divergence and speciation are often coupled (Rabosky and Adams, 2012), connecting biomechanics to morphological evolution enriches our understanding of the processes shaping diversification.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rabosky and Adams, 2012.

claim: Four-bar linkages are closed-chain systems comprised of four rigid links that rotate to transmit motion and force.
source: Four-bar linkages are closed-chain systems comprised of four rigid links that rotate to transmit motion and force (Anker, 1974; Muller, 1996; Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Mechanical output of four-bar linkages is often measured in terms of kinematic transmission (KT), a simple metric that can quantify a tradeoff between displacement and force across different linkage configurations.
source: Mechanical output of four-bar linkages is often measured in terms of kinematic transmission (KT), a simple metric that can quantify a tradeoff between displacement and force across different linkage configurations (see Materials and methods section for further information about KT).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how KT is used as a metric, with reference to further details in Materials and methods.

claim: Four-bar linkages are widespread in nature, and enable a rich diversity of behaviors in vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Four-bar linkages are widespread in nature, and enable a rich diversity of behaviors in vertebrates and invertebrates (Westneat, 1990; Wainwright et al., 2005; Patek et al., 2007; Olsen and Westneat, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature documenting four-bar linkages across taxa.

claim: Four-bar linkages actuate mouth opening for suction feeding in fishes.
source: For example, four-bar linkages actuate mouth opening for suction feeding in fishes (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994; Muller, 1987), flexion and extension of the vertebrate knee (Hobson and Torfason, 1974), rapid strikes of the stomatopod raptorial appendage (Patek et al., 2004; Patek et al., 2007; McHenry et al., 2012; McHenry et al., 2016), and skull kinesis in birds (Hoese and Westneat, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of fish feeding mechanics.

claim: Four-bar linkages enable flexion and extension of the vertebrate knee.
source: For example, four-bar linkages actuate mouth opening for suction feeding in fishes (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994; Muller, 1987), flexion and extension of the vertebrate knee (Hobson and Torfason, 1974), rapid strikes of the stomatopod raptorial appendage (Patek et al., 2004; Patek et al., 2007; McHenry et al., 2012; McHenry et al., 2016), and skull kinesis in birds (Hoese and Westneat, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hobson and Torfason, 1974.

claim: Four-bar linkages enable rapid strikes of the stomatopod raptorial appendage.
source: For example, four-bar linkages actuate mouth opening for suction feeding in fishes (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994; Muller, 1987), flexion and extension of the vertebrate knee (Hobson and Torfason, 1974), rapid strikes of the stomatopod raptorial appendage (Patek et al., 2004; Patek et al., 2007; McHenry et al., 2012; McHenry et al., 2016), and skull kinesis in birds (Hoese and Westneat, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of mantis shrimp strike mechanics.

claim: Four-bar linkages enable skull kinesis in birds.
source: For example, four-bar linkages actuate mouth opening for suction feeding in fishes (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994; Muller, 1987), flexion and extension of the vertebrate knee (Hobson and Torfason, 1974), rapid strikes of the stomatopod raptorial appendage (Patek et al., 2004; Patek et al., 2007; McHenry et al., 2012; McHenry et al., 2016), and skull kinesis in birds (Hoese and Westneat, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoese and Westneat, 1996.

claim: Four-bar linkages exhibit many-to-one mapping, meaning that similar mechanical outputs can be produced through different combinations of morphology.
source: Four-bar linkages, like any system built of three or more parts, exhibit many-to-one mapping, meaning that similar mechanical outputs (e.g. KT) can be produced through different combinations of morphology (e.g. link lengths; Wainwright et al., 2005; Wainwright, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wainwright et al., 2005 and Wainwright, 2007.

claim: Four-bar linkages exhibit mechanical sensitivity, which occurs when KT is disproportionately sensitive to variation in some links and relatively insensitive to variation in others.
source: Four-bar linkages also exhibit mechanical sensitivity, which occurs when KT is disproportionately sensitive to variation in some links and relatively insensitive to variation in others (Anderson and Patek, 2015; Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Patek, 2015 and Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: The mantis shrimp four-bar system is used for feeding, fighting, and substrate manipulation via extremely rapid strikes of their raptorial appendages.
source: The mantis shrimp four-bar system is used for feeding, fighting, and substrate manipulation via extremely rapid strikes of their raptorial appendages (Patek et al., 2004;Patek et al., 2007; Patek et al., 2013; Patek and Caldwell, 2005; McHenry et al., 2016; deVries et al., 2012; Green and Patek, 2015; Green and Patek, 2018; Crane et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of mantis shrimp behavior.

claim: Spearing stomatopods that harpoon mobile, soft-bodied prey have higher KT (greater displacement) than smashing mantis shrimp that bludgeon hard-shelled prey using linkages with lower KT (greater force).
source: Spearing stomatopods that harpoon mobile, soft-bodied prey have higher KT (greater displacement) than smashing mantis shrimp that bludgeon hard-shelled prey using linkages with lower KT (greater force) (Anderson et al., 2014; McHenry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2014 and McHenry et al., 2016.

claim: In mantis shrimp, the link most tightly correlated with KT exhibits the fastest rate of evolution.
source: In mantis shrimp, mechanical sensitivity is associated with accelerated evolution: the link most tightly correlated with KT exhibits the fastest rate of evolution (Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: In each four-bar system studied, stronger correlations between link lengths and kinematic transmission (KT) were associated with faster rates of morphological evolution.
source: A single consistent result emerged from our analysis of evolutionary rates: stronger correlations between link lengths and kinematic transmission (KT) were associated with faster rates of morphological evolution. In each system, we found that mechanical sensitivity was always associated with a faster rate of link evolution (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A higher evolutionary rate was not driven by greater variance in the traits studied.
source: Evolutionary rate can be artificially inflated by greater trait variance (O'Meara et al., 2006; Adams, 2013); we incorporated intraspecific measurement error into our rate estimates and confirmed that a higher evolutionary rate was not driven by greater variance (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by analyses that incorporated measurement error, with results shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output was positively correlated with input link length (PGLS r2=0.62, p<10−6).
source: For example, in the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output was positively correlated with input link length (PGLS r2=0.62, p<10−6), inversely correlated with the coupler link length (r2=0.27, p=0.002), and exhibited no relationship with the output link length (Supplementary file 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results shown in Table 1.

claim: In the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output was inversely correlated with the coupler link length (r2=0.27, p=0.002).
source: For example, in the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output was positively correlated with input link length (PGLS r2=0.62, p<10−6), inversely correlated with the coupler link length (r2=0.27, p=0.002), and exhibited no relationship with the output link length (Supplementary file 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results shown in Table 1.

claim: In the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output exhibited no relationship with the output link length.
source: For example, in the cichlid oral four-bar system, mechanical output was positively correlated with input link length (PGLS r2=0.62, p<10−6), inversely correlated with the coupler link length (r2=0.27, p=0.002), and exhibited no relationship with the output link length (Supplementary file 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results shown in Table 1.

claim: In the wrasse oral four-bar, the sunfish opercular four-bar, and the stomatopod raptorial four-bar, the output link length was a strong predictor of mechanical output (PGLS r2>0.66, p<10−11).
source: By contrast, in three systems - the wrasse oral four-bar, the sunfish opercular four-bar, and the stomatopod raptorial four-bar - the output link length was a strong predictor of mechanical output (PGLS r2>0.66, p<10−11), whereas the coupler link only weakly predicted mechanical output (PGLS r2<0.14) (Supplementary files 4–6).
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results referenced in Supplementary files 4-6.

claim: In the wrasse oral four-bar, the sunfish opercular four-bar, and the stomatopod raptorial four-bar, the coupler link only weakly predicted mechanical output (PGLS r2<0.14).
source: By contrast, in three systems - the wrasse oral four-bar, the sunfish opercular four-bar, and the stomatopod raptorial four-bar - the output link length was a strong predictor of mechanical output (PGLS r2>0.66, p<10−11), whereas the coupler link only weakly predicted mechanical output (PGLS r2<0.14) (Supplementary files 4–6).
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results referenced in Supplementary files 4-6.

claim: The oral four-bars of cichlids and wrasses share a common evolutionary origin.
source: The oral four-bars of cichlids and wrasses share a common evolutionary origin (Alfaro et al., 2004); nonetheless, rate differences were predicted by mechanical sensitivity rather than shared ancestry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alfaro et al., 2004.

claim: Rate differences in the oral four-bars of cichlids and wrasses were predicted by mechanical sensitivity rather than shared ancestry.
source: The oral four-bars of cichlids and wrasses share a common evolutionary origin (Alfaro et al., 2004); nonetheless, rate differences were predicted by mechanical sensitivity rather than shared ancestry.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing different patterns of mechanical sensitivity in cichlids and wrasses despite their shared ancestry.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity is consistently a strong predictor of evolutionary rate differences across four-bar linkage systems.
source: Hence, analogous four-bar systems do not result in common patterns of mechanical sensitivity, whereas mechanical sensitivity is consistently a strong predictor of evolutionary rate differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistent patterns observed across all four systems studied.

claim: Three well-supported evolutionary shifts in KT were detected in wrasses (posterior probability range 0.65–0.99).
source: We detected three well-supported evolutionary shifts in KT (posterior probability [pp] range 0.65–0.99; Supplementary file 7) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 7.

claim: For each of the three shifts in KT in wrasses, strongly supported shifts in the output and input links were detected, but never the coupler link.
source: For each of these shifts in mechanical output, we also detected strongly supported shifts in the output and input links, but never the coupler link (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three shifts in KT in wrasses occur through three different morphological pathways, but only via changes in the links to which KT is most mechanically sensitive.
source: Therefore, the three shifts in KT occur through three different morphological pathways, but only via the changes in the links to which KT is most mechanically sensitive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Bayesian analysis results showing shifts in different links (input and/or output) accompanying each KT shift.

claim: In razorfishes, the transition to higher KT is accompanied by a shift to a smaller output link (pp = 0.88).
source: In razorfishes, the transition to higher KT is accompanied by a shift to a smaller output link (pp = 0.88), and in Creole wrasse, by both an increase in input link length (pp = 0.97) and a reduction in output link length (pp = 0.77).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Creole wrasse (Clepticus parrae), the transition to higher KT is accompanied by both an increase in input link length (pp = 0.97) and a reduction in output link length (pp = 0.77).
source: In razorfishes, the transition to higher KT is accompanied by a shift to a smaller output link (pp = 0.88), and in Creole wrasse, by both an increase in input link length (pp = 0.97) and a reduction in output link length (pp = 0.77).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: A transition to lower KT in the Anampses clade is accompanied by a reduction in input link length (pp = 0.95), with no concomitant shifts in output link length.
source: A transition to lower KT in the Anampses clade is accompanied by a reduction in input link length (pp = 0.95), with no concomitant shifts in output link length.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Greater mechanical sensitivity is associated with faster morphological evolution in every four-bar linkage system tested.
source: Amidst the morphological, behavioral and ecological diversity of four-bar linkages, in every system we tested, greater mechanical sensitivity is associated with faster morphological evolution.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding, supported by data from all four systems studied.

claim: The connection between mechanical sensitivity and evolutionary rate is robust to independent origins and distinct behavioral functions.
source: The connection between mechanical sensitivity and evolutionary rate is therefore robust to independent origins and distinct behavioral functions, suggesting a generalizable phenomenon in four-bar linkage systems.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistent patterns observed across four independently evolved systems with different functions.

claim: Strong correlations between components and mechanical output accelerate evolutionary change.
source: These findings address a longstanding conundrum of constraints in evolution (discussed in Gould, 1989; Antonovics and van Tienderen, 1991; Schwenk, 1994) – specifically, whether strong correlations among traits should enhance or reduce evolutionary change – by demonstrating that strong correlations between components and mechanical output accelerate evolutionary change (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing faster evolutionary rates in links with stronger correlations to KT.

claim: The same length change applied to small and large links is proportionally larger for the small link, such that KT is most influenced by the change to the small link.
source: In terms of absolute size, the same length change applied to small and large links is proportionally larger for the small link, such that KT is most influenced by the change to the small link.
evidence: This is a biomechanical explanation based on geometric principles of four-bar linkages.

claim: Changes to the smallest links induce disproportionately large changes in the system's geometry and, therefore, the transmission of force and motion.
source: Therefore, changes to the smallest links induce disproportionately large changes in the system's geometry and, therefore, the transmission of force and motion (Anderson and Patek, 2015; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Patek, 2015 and Hu et al., 2017.

claim: Greater disparity among link sizes in a four-bar system results in greater evolutionary rate disparity.
source: In terms of relative size, greater disparity among link sizes in a four-bar system results in greater evolutionary rate disparity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the patterns in different systems, particularly stomatopods and sunfish versus cichlids and wrasses.

claim: In the stomatopod raptorial four-bar linkage and sunfish opercular four-bar linkage, the output link is approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the input and coupler links, and it also exhibits an order of magnitude faster evolution.
source: These effects of size are especially apparent in the stomatopod raptorial four-bar linkage and sunfish opercular four-bar linkage. In both of these systems, the output link is approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the input and coupler links, and it also exhibits an order of magnitude faster evolution (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity biases evolutionary transitions to traits with the greatest influence on mechanical output (input and output links).
source: Our findings in wrasses, however, demonstrate that mechanical sensitivity biases evolutionary transitions to traits with the greatest influence on mechanical output (input and output links).
evidence: This is supported by the Bayesian analysis of trait shifts in wrasses shown in Figure 3.

claim: For each of the three major KT shifts in wrasses, three distinct morphological pathways were detected involving either the input link, output link, or both (but never the coupler link).
source: For each of the three major KT shifts in wrasses, we detected three distinct morphological pathways involving either the input link, output link, or both (but never the coupler link).
evidence: This is supported by the Bayesian analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both the output link and input link are strong predictors of KT in the wrasse oral four-bar, and the coupler is a weak predictor of KT.
source: Correspondingly, both the output link and input link are strong predictors of KT in the wrasse oral four-bar, and the coupler is a weak predictor of KT.
evidence: This is supported by PGLS regression results for the wrasse system.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity restricts the freedom of evolution central to many-to-one mapping by biasing evolutionary transitions to traits with the strongest effect on mechanical output.
source: Therefore, mechanical sensitivity restricts the freedom of evolution central to many-to-one mapping by biasing evolutionary transitions to traits with the strongest effect on mechanical output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that trait shifts occur only in mechanically sensitive links despite the theoretical possibility of many-to-one mapping.

claim: Mantis shrimp use their shortest link (output link) to dramatically amplify an approximately nine-degree rotation of the input link, enabling the notoriously fast angular velocity of their predatory appendages.
source: Mantis shrimp use their shortest link (output link) to dramatically amplify an approximately nine-degree rotation of the input link; this enables the notoriously fast angular velocity of their predatory appendages (Patek et al., 2004,Patek et al., 2007; Cox et al., 2014; McHenry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of mantis shrimp strike mechanics.

claim: In centrarchids, linkage geometry is used to amplify gape because the input rotation is controlled by a muscle too small to generate a large gape.
source: In the centrarchids, the input rotation is controlled by a muscle too small to generate a large gape: instead they use linkage geometry to amplify gape (Durie and Turingan, 2004; Camp and Brainerd, 2015; Camp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of centrarchid feeding mechanics.

claim: The maxilla (output link) in the oral four-bar of teleosts is correlated with jaw protrusion, a key ecological aspect of fish diversification.
source: In the case of the oral four-bar of teleosts, the maxilla (output link) is correlated with jaw protrusion, a key ecological aspect of fish diversification (Hulsey and Garcia De Leon, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hulsey and Garcia De Leon, 2005.

claim: The most mechanically influential links may play a crucial role in shaping diversification during speciation and adaptive radiation.
source: As such, the most mechanically influential links may play a crucial role in shaping diversification during speciation and adaptive radiation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential broader implications of the findings.

claim: In the teleost oral four-bar system, the lower jaw (coronoid process - mandible-quadrate joint) functions as the input link and its rotation relative to the fixed link (suspensorium - neurocranium) causes outward rotation in the maxilla (output link), resulting in premaxillary protrusion.
source: In the teleost oral four-bar system, the lower jaw (coronoid process - mandible-quadrate joint) functions as the input link and its rotation relative to the fixed link (suspensorium - neurocranium) causes outward rotation in the maxilla (output link), resulting in premaxillary protrusion (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994).
evidence: This is a description of the teleost oral four-bar system supported by citations.

claim: In the teleost opercular four-bar linkage system, the operculum (input link) rotates relative to the suspensorium (fixed link), and this rotation transfers through the interopercle bone and the interopercle-mandible ligament (coupler link), and then to the retroarticular process of the mandible (output link).
source: In this case, the operculum (input link) rotates relative to the suspensorium (fixed link). This rotation transfers through the interopercle bone and the interopercle-mandible ligament (coupler link), and then to the retroarticular process of the mandible (output link).
evidence: This is a description of the teleost opercular four-bar system.

claim: Rotation of the output link in the teleost opercular four-bar actuates jaw depression, which contributes to the motion of the oral four-bar system that facilitates feeding via protrusion of the premaxilla.
source: Rotation of the output link actuates jaw depression, which also contributes to the motion of the oral four-bar system that facilitates feeding via protrusion of the premaxilla (Westneat, 1990; Martins, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westneat, 1990 and Martins, 1994.

claim: During a mantis shrimp strike, the input link (meral-V) rotates distally, relative to the rest of the merus (fixed link), and this distal rotation releases the stored elastic energy and pushes the carpus segment (output link), causing it to rotate and actuate the swinging arm.
source: During a mantis shrimp strike, the input link (meral-V) rotates distally, relative to the rest of the merus (fixed link) (Patek et al., 2007). This distal rotation releases the stored elastic energy, and pushes the carpus segment (output link), causing it to rotate and actuate the swinging arm.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Patek et al., 2007.

claim: The coupler of the mantis shrimp four-bar system is an extensor muscle that remains contracted during the strike.
source: The coupler of the system is an extensor muscle that remains contracted during the strike.
evidence: This is a description of the mantis shrimp four-bar system.

claim: The wrasse morphological and biomechanical dataset is comprised of 101 species from 32 genera.
source: The wrasse morphological and biomechanical dataset (Alfaro et al., 2004) is comprised of 101 species from 32 genera that we pruned down from 122 species using a recent time-calibrated phylogeny (Baliga and Law, 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The cichlid morphological and biomechanical dataset is comprised of 30 species from 13 genera.
source: The cichlid morphological and biomechanical dataset (Hulsey and Garcia De Leon, 2005) is comprised of 30 species from 13 genera, which we pruned down from the 97 species represented in a recent time-calibrated mitochondrial phylogeny (Hulsey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The sunfish dataset consists of morphological and biomechanical data for 19 species from eight genera.
source: The sunfish dataset (Hu et al., 2017) consists of morphological and biomechanical data for 19 species from eight genera.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The stomatopod morphological and biomechanical dataset consisted of 36 species from six superfamilies.
source: The stomatopod morphological and biomechanical dataset (Anderson and Patek, 2015) consisted of 36 species from six superfamilies.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: KT is calculated as the ratio of angular output motion relative to angular input motion.
source: KT is calculated as the ratio of angular output motion relative to angular input motion (Hulsey and Wainwright, 2002).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation.

claim: All else being equal, KT reflects a tradeoff between displacement and force: a higher KT yields greater displacement through more output rotation relative to input rotation, whereas lower KT yields greater force that occurs at the expense of displacement.
source: All else being equal, KT reflects a tradeoff between displacement and force: a higher KT yields greater displacement through more output rotation relative to input rotation, whereas lower KT yields greater force that occurs at the expense of displacement (Westneat, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Westneat, 1994.

claim: Non-planar motion occurs in some biological linkage systems and those systems should be studied as three-dimensional mechanisms.
source: Recent work demonstrates that non-planar motion occurs in some biological linkage systems and that those systems should be studied as three-dimensional mechanisms (Olsen and Westneat, 2016; Olsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olsen and Westneat, 2016 and Olsen et al., 2017.

claim: The effect of non-planar movement on calculations of KT varies among systems and is unlikely to be a major source of error in the systems examined in this study.
source: The effect of non-planar movement on calculations of KT varies among systems and is unlikely to be a major source of error in the systems examined here (Patek et al., 2007; McHenry et al., 2012,McHenry et al., 2016; Anderson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of the specific systems examined.

claim: KT is dynamic, meaning that its magnitude changes during the rotation of the input link.
source: Another issue is that KT is dynamic, meaning that its magnitude changes during the rotation of the input link (Patek et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Patek et al., 2007.

claim: In the wrasse and cichlid oral four-bar systems, KT was measured statically with the input link fixed at a starting angle of 30° in the lower-jaw rotation.
source: In two of the fish systems examined (oral four-bar in wrasses and cichlids), KT was measured statically, specifically with the input link fixed at a starting angle of 30° in the lower-jaw rotation.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in previous studies.

claim: The 30° starting angle for measuring KT in wrasses and cichlids was chosen because it is biologically relevant for fish feeding.
source: This angle was chosen because it is biologically relevant for fish feeding (Westneat, 1990), and because starting angle was less important than link length for determining KT (Wainwright et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westneat, 1990 and Wainwright et al., 2005.

claim: Starting angle was less important than link length for determining KT.
source: This angle was chosen because it is biologically relevant for fish feeding (Westneat, 1990), and because starting angle was less important than link length for determining KT (Wainwright et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wainwright et al., 2005.

claim: In the sunfish and the mantis shrimp, KT was calculated in a dynamic fashion, by measuring the minimum value of KT over the course of its full rotation.
source: In the sunfish and the mantis shrimp, KT was calculated in a dynamic fashion, by measuring the minimum value of KT over the course of its full rotation (Anderson and Patek, 2015; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used, supported by citations.

claim: Patterns of mechanical sensitivity were not impacted by the use of dynamic or static measures of KT.
source: We found that patterns of mechanical sensitivity were not impacted by the use of dynamic or static measures of KT (Supplementary file 16).
evidence: This is supported by analyses shown in Supplementary file 16.

claim: Estimates of mechanical sensitivity were robust to alternative size corrections.
source: Nonetheless, estimates of mechanical sensitivity were robust to alternative size corrections (Supplementary file 17).
evidence: This is supported by analyses shown in Supplementary file 17.
